title: Interop stability tactics, TF snippets, and rollback matrix
content:
Overview:
This note collects pragmatic tactics for migrating Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) to the new serving runtime and control-plane protocol while preserving API compatibility. Focus: minimize customer-visible errors, predictable rollback paths, Terraform module migration snippets, and a simple decision/rollback matrix to use during cutovers.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Private deployments where customers run the Redwood appliance or private control plane (VPC mode or on-prem appliance).
- Target change set: runtime binary bump (v2.x), control-plane protocol update (gRPC -> framed gRPC v2), and accompanying TF module inputs that rename a few fields.
- Customers may run heterogeneous hardware (A100, H100); kernel selection differences exist.
- We assume CI builds provide image: registry.redwood.ai/private-runtime:v2-20241010 and control-plane:v2-20241010.

High-level strategy (phases):
Phase 0 — Readiness and safety hooks (preparation, non-disruptive)
- Inventory: run infra-scan to list clusters, kernel versions, GPU types, tfstate owners, and API clients (api-compat-checker).
- Create a migration ticket per customer with owner, blast radius, and rollback lead.
- Add feature flag gate in control-plane: "enable_v2_protocol" default off.
- Snapshot TF state and backup S3 buckets and DBs (daily retention).

Phase 1 — Shadow control-plane and compatibility shim
- Deploy control-plane:v2 in shadow mode: it accepts v1 control traffic but logs compatibility mismatches.
- Start canary runtime nodes in v2 with disabled routing — attach to shadow control-plane only.
- Run integration tests: token generation, streaming, KV cache reuse, and long-context replay.

Phase 2 — Canary and progressive traffic shift
- Enable v2 protocol for a narrow canary cohort (internal tenants or low-traffic customers).
- Gradually increase traffic (10% -> 25% -> 50%) while monitoring errors, latency p95, and token cost delta.
- Have automatic fallback to v1 control-plane and runtime variant if error rate exceeds threshold.

Phase 3 — Broad roll and cleanup
- Flip feature flag, migrate TF module references (see snippets below), and schedule a low-impact maintenance window for customers with strict SLAs.
- Run final verification and remove shadow copies.

Pre-req checklist (quick):
- [ ] tfstate backup verified and stored
- [ ] DB snapshot and retention policy validated
- [ ] Monitoring dashboards created (p95 latency, error-rate, compatibility mismatch log rate)
- [ ] Rollback runbook published per cluster
- [ ] Customer comms plan drafted (timeline, potential impacts)

API compatibility gating matrix (simplified):
- Breaking change category A: request/response schema removal (requires client update).
- Category B: header/metadata rename (shim possible in control-plane for 30 days).
- Category C: deprecated fields (safe, no client work required).

Gating rules:
- If Category A is present for a customer, mark them "manual migration" and schedule per-customer update.
- For Category B, enable control-plane shim for a max of 30 days while emailing affected customers.

Terraform module migration notes (practical snippets):
- Goal: make module changes non-breaking and additive, provide a compatibility wrapper module.
- Strategy: add new arguments with "deprecate_" flags then promote. Keep old inputs working by mapping them to new ones.

Example snippet (compat wrapper):
```
module "private_controlplane_compat" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//private-controlplane?ref=main"

  # new preferred flag
  protocol_version = var.protocol_version != null ? var.protocol_version : lookup(var.legacy_inputs, "protocol_version", "v1")

  # map renamed field
  node_pool_name = var.node_pool_name != null ? var.node_pool_name : var.legacy_nodepool

  # keep explicit provider pinning for heterogenous hw
  providers = { aws = aws.primary }
}
```
Notes: encourage customers to pass protocol_version when ready. Add a migration script in repo that runs "terraform state mv" for renamed resources where necessary.

Terraform state migration commands (examples):
- Identify resource: terraform state list | grep private_controlplane
- Move resource: terraform state mv module.old_name.aws_instance.foo module.new_name.aws_instance.foo
- Always run mv in a maintenance window and with remote state lock enabled.

Runtime kernel/quantization compatibility tactics:
- Provide per-model kernel profiles (models/*.yaml) and ship with defaults that prefer conservative FP16 kernels on older cards.
- Expose an env var REDWOOD_FORCE_KERNEL=fallback for canary nodes to force legacy kernel path if OOMs occur.

Rollback decision matrix (condensed):
- Trigger: error rate above 1% or p95 latency > 2x baseline for 5m.
- Immediate rollback: disable v2 feature flag in control-plane (instant), then scale down v2 runtime nodes.
- If TF input changes were applied (variables renamed), run the TF compatibility wrapper to re-map inputs and run terraform apply to restore previous resource names.
- For state rename mistakes: run terraform state mv back to original paths. Keep a tested script for common rename patterns.

Rollback commands (cheat sheet):
- Control-plane flag flip (k8s): kubectl -n redwood patch cm control-plane-flags -p '{"data":{"enable_v2_protocol":"false"}}'
- Scale runtime: kubectl -n redwood scale deploy/runtime-v2 --replicas=0
- TF revert (if plan approved earlier): git checkout -- modules/private-controlplane/main.tf && terraform apply -target=module.private_controlplane -auto-approve

Test plan (must-pass gates):
- Smoke: token create, short completion, streaming handshake.
- Integration: chat-context preservation, KV cache lookups across requests, model selection routing.
- Load: 95th percentile latency within 1.5x of baseline at expected qps for 10m windows.
- Data integrity: no dropped request bodies, end-to-end request IDs preserved.

Monitoring and runbook alerts to create:
- compatibility_mismatch_rate > 0.1% over 1h
- runtime_oom_rate > 0 for 10m on any node
- p95_latency_increase > 2x baseline for 5m
- tfstate_lock_failures > 0 (block further TF applies)

Post-migration validation checklist (first 72h):
- [ ] All canaries promoted or rolled back as expected
- [ ] No semantic API errors reported by customers
- [ ] DB and cache hit rates within expected variance
- [ ] Control-plane logs show <0.01% compatibility shims used (if shims were enabled)

Known risks and mitigations (brief):
- Risk: state rename leads to drift and resource duplication. Mitigation: require state mv rehearsal in a staging copy of tfstate and include idempotent rollback script.
- Risk: kernel incompat (OOM) on older GPUs. Mitigation: conservative default kernel, REDWOOD_FORCE_KERNEL env, and a per-model profile.
- Risk: clients using internal headers. Mitigation: control-plane shim and customer outreach.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Define retention timeline for compatibility shims (propose 30 days).
- Add automated tfstate "dry run" tool that validates resource name changes against live state.
- Draft customer notification templates for Category B header renames.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting tips
- If control-plane refuses to accept nodes: check TLS cert rotation (common corner case).
- If terraform apply fails with provider version mismatch: pin provider versions in module and run 'terraform init -upgrade=false'.

This doc is intentionally pragmatic — keep notes here as we iterate. Use per-customer tickets to capture anomalies and update this doc with lessons learned after each migration.
